summary.headline: The domain root delivers only 202 characters of visible text -- a title and an explicit 'Javascript is required for this site' notice -- with no noscript fallback, even though the platform's actual content (item pages) renders fine without JavaScript — medium severity, Server-render a real description of the organization and its holdings at the domain root, or add a noscript fallback with equivalent content.

findings.title: The domain root delivers only 202 characters of visible text -- a title and an explicit 'Javascript is required for this site' notice -- with no noscript fallback, even though the platform's actual content (item pages) renders fine without JavaScript
findings.evidence: A plain fetch to https://archive.org/ returns HTTP 200 but reduces to 202 characters after stripping markup: the page title plus 'Javascript is required for this site. Consider enabling Javascript or upgrading to a modern browser.' Zero JSON-LD, no meta description beyond the title tag, no noscript fallback of any kind. This is narrower than the site-wide SPA gaps found on other sites in this project's history (khanacademy.org, duolingo.com): sampled item pages under /details/ deliver full, substantial text (5,000+ characters, real metadata) without any JavaScript dependency at all, so the platform's actual archived content is not blocked -- only the homepage, the entry point most likely to be the first and only page a casual crawl or citation ever reaches, is affected.

reproduction.observed: 202 characters: title plus a 'Javascript is required' notice, no other content
reproduction.expected: A description of what the Internet Archive is and does, comparable in substance to what item pages already deliver without JavaScript

suggested_action.summary: Server-render a real description of the organization and its holdings at the domain root, or add a noscript fallback with equivalent content.
suggested_action.mechanism: An assistant or crawler that starts at the domain root -- the most common entry point for any site -- currently gets nothing to work with about what the Internet Archive is, even though the same non-executing fetch method works fine one click deeper on any item page.
steps: Add server-rendered descriptive text or a noscript fallback to the homepage template.
suggested_action.verification: A plain fetch to https://archive.org/ returns substantive text describing the organization.

findings.title: Item pages -- the core content of the entire platform -- carry only a generic BreadcrumbList in JSON-LD, with zero CreativeWork/MediaObject-type schema, despite rich, complete descriptive metadata (title, creator, publication date, media type, description) already present as plain visible text on the same page
findings.evidence: Two sampled item pages (/details/<identifier>, one an audio item, one a different media type) each carry exactly one JSON-LD block: a BreadcrumbList naming only the top-level category (e.g. 'Audio'). Neither carries any CreativeWork, MediaObject, Book, or equivalent schema.org node describing the item itself. Yet the same page's visible text states the item's full title ('Pride & Prejudice by Queer Sounds'), publication date ('2020-06-24'), topic/category, a substantive description, and access-restriction status -- all facts a CreativeWork node exists specifically to carry. Internet Archive's own metadata API (/metadata/<identifier>) already exposes this exact data in structured form for internal use; none of it reaches the page's own JSON-LD.

reproduction.observed: Only 'BreadcrumbList' and 'ListItem' on both sampled items
reproduction.expected: A CreativeWork (or the more specific Book/MovieObject/AudioObject/MediaObject) node stating name, creator, datePublished and description, matching what the metadata API and the page's own visible text already state

suggested_action.summary: Emit a CreativeWork-family JSON-LD node on item detail pages, populated directly from the existing /metadata/<identifier> API response.
suggested_action.mechanism: An assistant citing an archived work today has no structured source for its title, creator, date or licensing status, and must fall back to unreliable prose extraction from a page whose visible layout is oriented toward human browsing (icons, action buttons, borrow/download controls) rather than a clean statement of the work's identity -- despite the underlying structured metadata already existing and being one API call away.
steps: Map the existing /metadata/<identifier> fields (title, creator, date, mediatype, description, licenseurl) onto a CreativeWork or media-type-specific JSON-LD node.
Add this node to the item detail page template.
Verify the emitted title/date match the page's own visible text exactly.
suggested_action.verification: A sample of item pages across different media types (audio, text, video) each carry a CreativeWork-family node whose fields match the page's visible metadata.

not_assessed.check: Answerability, freshness/corroboration, and engagement; structured data across other item media types (text/books, video, web captures via the Wayback Machine specifically)
not_assessed.reason: This run hand-verified two audio item pages plus the homepage rather than sampling broadly across the platform's very wide range of content types (books, video, software, web archive snapshots).
not_assessed.impact: Cannot say whether the missing-CreativeWork-schema finding holds identically for Wayback Machine capture pages specifically, which have a different template and purpose from a media item page.

not_assessed.reason: No headless-browser engine (Playwright/Puppeteer) was available in this run's environment.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot assess the actual on-site experience for a JavaScript-executing visitor, including whether the homepage's JS-dependent content is itself fast or well-built once it loads.
